newsitem.title: USA: Minor Metals says cobalt lawsuits were last resort.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals says cobalt lawsuits were last resort.

text.p: Minor Metals Inc, said its two lawsuits filed against the Defense National Stockpile Center concerning U.S. government stockpiled cobalt sales, were a last resort.
"MMI has believed, for a very long time, that it has not been treated fairly by DNSC (Stockpile) and it has tried to amicably resolve its concerns with DNSC," the company said in a statement.
It was Minor Metals' first public comment on the lawsuits which have suspended U.S. Stockpile cobalt sales, helping the market to move higher, according to some traders.
"It has turned to litigation only as a last resort," MMI added.
Minor Metals, also known as Metals Resources Group Ltd, detailed the two lawsuits currently underway.

In U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, MMI said its complaint includes that DNSC improperly moved, in Solicitation 004 (February's negotiated sale offer), from a first best and final offer (BAFO) to a second BAFO.
"DNSC has never before held a second BAFO in cobalt or any other commodity," MMI said.
MMI added that DNSC failed to hold meaningful negotiations with MMI, after first BAFO, or disclose to it the evaluation criteria DNSC used to evalutate second BAFOs.

"DNSC has effectively barred MMI from all cobalt sales subsequent to the award to MMI of 1,898,487 pounds cobalt contained, in August 1995, and 1,257,064 pounds cobalt contained, awarded in December 1995," MMI said.
The court issued a temporary restraining order prohibiting DNSC from releasing additional material to awardees until the court has made its judgement.
The trial will likely be held in early May, MMI added.
Due to the District Court trial, two protest against the Stockpile previously lodged by MMI with the General Accounting Office have been dismissed.
The second court case is in the United States Court of Federal Claims where MMI has argued that DNSC acted against the law on three accounts.

DNSC prohibited all or none bids when selling cobalt, used a best value award criterion in the context of a sealed bid offering in which price alone should be the award criterion, and used a domestic preference evaluation scheme that is not authorized by law, MMI said in its statement.
DNSC was directed by the Federal Claims court on April 3 not to conduct any future cobalt sales until it has ruled on the merits of the complaint.
"The judge indicated that the case should be decided by late May or early June 1997," MMI said.
